item.title: A Death in the Family — Karl Ove Knausgård
item.description:
PREFACE

This review was originally written on January 15th, 2025. I'm not particularly happy with it, as is so often the case with my writing, and I fully intend to rewrite it in the future. Nevertheless, the original text is being kept here for archival purposes.

I first encountered the work of Karl Ove Knausgård whilst I was browsing the shelves at my local bookshop; there, a lone copy of the final entry in his ‘My Struggle’ series, aptly named ‘The End’, caught my eye, and after scanning the book’s pages for only a moment, I made a mental note, went home, and promptly ordered the entirety of the series.

item.title: On Smoking
item.description:
CONTENT WARNING: THIS PAGE CONTAINS REFERENCES TO SELF-HARM.

I never thought that I would grow up to be a smoker. The broad, sweeping landscape of memories from my childhood — so alien to me, now — cherry-picks recollections of days spent without rhyme, reason, or structure; of my brother, my mother, or my father at random; and feeds them to me with an unsteady, coltish hand. By and large, these memories are pleasant ones and not at all unwelcome, with each and every one of them coloured, naturally, by my perception of these events, but also by more fluid concepts and hazy meanings attached to the people in them; in the case of my father, for example, my view of him is dictated by a core set of strangely complimentary tones: the elusive, seemingly forever out-of-reach pedestal of masculinity, safety, and guidance that comes with being a father; my own desire, particularly as I grew, to climb up alongside him atop that peculiar throne to stand, side-by-side, as equals; and the cloying smell of second-hand smoke that has come to suffuse each and every memory with an offensive odour that blurs his figure and shrouds him in a thick, enigmatic haze.

item.title: Choosing a Palette
item.description: When it comes to choosing a palette for a project, there are too many options. A lot of these options and choices are naturally narrowed down by the both the core of the project and its scope; pixel art, for example, allows for the use of a breadth of colours — various shades, highlights, and supporting hues — to set the tone or convey a particular feeling or mood. When it comes to designing websites, however, there’s rarely any need (other than for an a bit of artistic flair, perhaps) to have more than a few base colours.

item.title: Reading for the Sake of Writing
item.description: I don’t read as much as I should. I have stacks upon stacks of books — spilling out of a bookshelf and across my desk, my coffee table, my other shelves — that are, for the most part, unread. Like many readers, I have a peculiar habit of frequently adding to my library and never quite catching up with it, and the time that I actually set aside for reading is becoming less and less.

item.title: Building arscorvi.github.io
item.description:
I like making websites.

I’ve always liked making websites. I wouldn’t necessarily consider myself a designer, developer, or coder — these are all words that I would use to describe someone who does this with much more frequency and demonstrable ability than I do — but I do enjoy making private little corners of the internet for my things. When it comes to languages, HTML and CSS are the ones that I am most familiar with for as long as I can remember; I used my rudimentary understanding of these languages as far back as the age of 14-years-old to design various little blurbs and rulesets for the games that I played and hosted, and that knowledge never really went away.
